title: The trades don't lie
text:
The story is what happened after, when I stopped trading and started reading. Every trade in the competition is recorded on-chain. The winners couldn't hide how they did it, and once I looked, they told me exactly why I lost.

What I built

The event was the Gensyn Delphi Agent Arena: autonomous agents trading test tokens on prediction markets, ranked by profit, top three split a cash pool.

My agent, kazani-oracle, was a TypeScript loop running on GitHub Actions every few minutes. Each tick it pulled the open markets, researched every question with a web-grounded LLM (Perplexity Sonar, which searches the live web inside a single call), turned that into a probability, and, when the probability disagreed with the market price by enough, placed a bet on-chain and held it to settlement.

The plumbing worked on the first live tick: ten real on-chain trades, fills within spec, nobody at the keyboard. It ran untouched for two weeks. If you'd asked me on day one whether I'd built a real trading agent, the answer was yes.

Plumbing isn't edge

Day one I slid down the leaderboard. Not because my predictions were wrong, but because the agent kept re-buying the same thin markets every tick, and each re-entry paid the spread again. I was bleeding slippage, not losing bets. One rule fixed it: bet each market once, then hold. The bleed stopped and profit crawled back to positive.

Positive on test tokens is not winning. I finished around 48th of 107. Plus 67 tokens. The people who won did plus twelve thousand.

This is the part I keep circling. I had solved the hard-looking problem, an autonomous agent that trades real markets on-chain, and completely missed the real one: being right, and betting like it. The plumbing was never the hard part. Anyone with the SDK could build what I built.

Reading the winners trades

The normal move here is to shrug, close the tab, and go find the next competition. I didn't want to. I wanted to know why they won, and for once I had the full record. Every buy, every sell, every settlement, permanent and public on-chain.

So I built a second tool. Give it a wallet address and it reconstructs that wallet's entire competition from the chain's index: every trade, position sizes, entry timing, win rate, realized profit.

I didn't have the winners' addresses. The leaderboard shows names, not wallets. But it shows profit and trade counts, and those turned out to be fingerprints. Only one wallet made 12,967 across exactly 129 trades. Match the number, you've found the person. I found all three.

The four gaps

Here is what the chain showed.

Three completely different ways to win. Jamport barely traded: 10 markets, huge size, went all-in on one, and was right every single time. Ramalogy spread wider and pressed winners hard, betting more than twice the starting bankroll on conviction. tolègba made markets, 1,541 small trades grinding the spread. No shared strategy.

One shared trait: a real edge, sized like they believed it.

I had neither. My win rate was a coin flip. And my bet size, 15 tokens a trade because I'd clamped it to stop the day-one bleed, meant even the markets I got right paid me almost nothing. Egg prices, CPI, "will this product ship by Friday: no", I called the same ones Jamport did. He put the bankroll on them. I put pocket change.

The discipline that saved me on day one is the discipline that capped me for the next thirteen. Small and safe is how you avoid losing. It isn't how you win.

The part that actually paid

I wrote all of this up and sent it to the team as feedback. Not my profit, my read of it: what I built, what broke, what the winners did differently, what I'd change before risking real money.

That's what converted. They replied, invited me onto their X Space, and then picked me for a paid interview about the winning strategies. The mid-pack finisher got the same seat as the winners, because I'd studied the game instead of only playing it.

Which is the point, shrunk down. I handed the trading to an agent and it lost. I kept the understanding, and the understanding is what got paid. The agent was the replaceable part.

If you're building agents to act for you, that's the split worth watching. Let the machine do the work. Keep the understanding for yourself.

I build small things solo and write up what I learn. The agent, the winner-analysis tool, and the full teardown aren't public yet, but I'm happy to share the code and walk anyone through it.

title: Before You Buy the ₹28,500 Ring: The Health Dashboard Your Dadi Already Gave You
text:
The ring is in your cart. Titanium, matte black, good reviews. You've done the math on the ₹28,500 and told yourself it isn't a gadget, it's an investment in finally knowing your own body. Sleep depth, recovery, the metabolic stuff. Real numbers, at last, instead of guessing.

Wait before you tap Buy.

Almost everything that ring is about to measure has been sitting inside your body this whole time. Your grandmother could read most of it without charging anything overnight. She didn't call it HRV. She looked at your face and knew you'd slept badly. She watched you push your plate away and knew your digestion was off. No app, no subscription, no score to make you anxious about the score.

That's not nostalgia. It's the argument this piece makes.

I almost bought it too

I was the target customer. Three tabs open, Ultrahuman versus Oura versus just-buy-the-Apple-Watch, cart loaded, finger hovering for days. What gave me pause wasn't willpower. It was a plain observation most of us from an Indian household can make: there is usually someone at home who reads the body without a single gadget. They take one look at your face and know you slept badly. They watch you leave half your plate and know your digestion is off. Usually right before any number would have flagged it.

That left me with a question I couldn't shake. Is tracking the same as knowing?

I'm not a Vaidya (Ayurvedic doctor), and I'm not against technology, I work with it. But I was about to pay for a skill that was arguably already in the house, sitting in a tradition most of us had quietly filed under "grandmother stuff." The grandmother stuff has names, a system, and about five thousand years of field notes.

What you'll walk away with

Three things. What that ring actually measures, and why it's a skill you can build rather than a substance you buy. Four things Ayurveda formalised centuries ago that today's wearables are now re-deriving at a premium. And how to run one of these reads tomorrow morning, before your feet touch the floor, for free.

None of this is an argument against buying the ring. It's an argument for knowing what you're buying first.

The problem was never data

Something quiet has happened to a lot of us. We've started feeling like we can't trust our own sense of our health until a number confirms it. You slept fine, the app says 61, and now the day feels off. The reflex fix is better tech, cheaper tech: wait for the ring to get affordable, democratise the data, sorted.

That skips what the device actually does. It doesn't hand you the skill of reading your body. It replaces it, and often makes it worse. There's a clinical name for the sharp end of this, orthosomnia (sleep-tracker anxiety), where people buy a tracker to sleep better and sleep worse because the score itself becomes one more thing to worry about. The tool meant to fix the problem starts causing it.

Data was never the bottleneck. Interoception was: the trained ability to read your own internal signals. India didn't lack this. It built one of the most detailed systems for it anywhere, then got talked into buying the ability back at a premium. If the real asset is attention, the ring is a downgrade with an EMI plan.

Four translations make this concrete. Old idea on the left, the wearable chasing it on the right.

1. Agni: your metabolic dashboard

Agni (digestive fire) is the exact thing a continuous glucose monitor you re-buy every couple of weeks and a microbiome kit are trying to put a number on. Drop the Sanskrit and agni just means how cleanly you turn food into steady energy, and how well your gut runs from day to day.

You already have the readout. Eat your dal-chawal lunch and notice where you are ninety minutes later. Clear and steady, or foggy and reaching for chai and a nap? That crash is a glucose curve. You're reading it directly instead of through a sensor stuck in your arm. Add the second free signal: a daily, well-formed bowel movement, ideally around the same time. That's your microbiome report, and it costs nothing.

Tomorrow, clock your energy ninety minutes after lunch. One honest read.

Agni tells you how you process the world. The next reading tells you how much reserve you have to withstand it.

2. Ojas: your recovery score

Ojas (vital reserve) is the buffer that decides whether a bad night, a heavy wedding meal, or a brutal week at work flattens you or barely lands. That buffer is what a Whoop recovery percentage gestures at, and what inflammatory blood panels chase after the fact.

The free version is one question. How many days do you take to bounce back? A hard workout, a dodgy restaurant meal, a stressful stretch: does a small hit knock you out for two or three days, or do you reset by morning? Resilience is the metric, not a number, and ojas named that idea long before recovery got a dashboard.

After your next stressor, count the bounce-back days. Honestly.

Reserve shows up over days. The next signal you read the moment you wake.

3. The morning read: nadi, tongue, first light

The old morning self-check is what Ayurveda calls nadi pariksha (pulse reading), plus a look at the tongue, the first bowel movement, and the quality of your waking mind. It's the original version of the sleep report you thumb through before your feet hit the floor.

These are the body's overnight status lights. Can you hold your attention for thirty minutes after waking, no fog, no headache? That's a cleaner read on sleep quality than any stage graph. How settled is your head before caffeine, before the phone, before the world gets a vote? That's your nervous system telling you where it's set this morning. The Oura report is this same inspection, the dinacharya (daily routine) morning check, dressed in biometrics.

Tomorrow, before you touch your phone, take sixty seconds. How clear is your head? What's your first honest read of your own body?

These reads only mean something inside a stable rhythm, which is the fourth translation, and the one no wearable can sell you.

4. Dinacharya: the foundations even the biohackers admit come first

Dinacharya means daily rhythm: a consistent wake time, morning light, regular meals, a real wind-down. Here's the tell. Even the most gadget-maximalist optimiser will admit these boring inputs matter more than any metric on any ring. Get your foundations right first, they say, or the fancy data is just noise.

That's a five-thousand-year-old instruction reached by process of elimination. It pairs with the deepest idea of the lot, prakriti (your individual constitution). The wearable sells one dashboard to everyone and calls the average "normal." Ayurveda started from the opposite end: your baseline is yours, learning it is the whole point, and measuring yourself against a stranger misses it.

Tomorrow, anchor one thing. Same wake time, or ten minutes of morning light.

Four translations, one pattern. Not one of them needs a battery.

The actual experiment

Don't turn this into a checklist you obsess over. That just rebuilds the same anxiety in a kurta. Do the opposite. Pick one signal.

Tonight, choose one of the four. New to this? Take the morning read. Highest signal, near-zero effort.

Tomorrow, before the phone, spend sixty seconds on that one read. Write it down, one line, on paper. Analog on purpose. No app.

After a week of the same single read, you'll have something no first-day device gives you: your own baseline. Not a population average, your normal.

Then refine. And if you still want the ring, buy it. Genuinely. You'll just know exactly what it's meant to confirm, which makes you the qualified user instead of the overquantified one. This was pre-purchase clarity, never a purity test.

One honest caution, because of where we live. This is about everyday self-knowledge in a healthy body. If you're managing a diagnosed condition, diabetes especially, and India has every reason to take that seriously, your doctor's tools are not the villain here. Read your body and keep your CGM. Different jobs.

The finger, still hovering

Back to the cart. The ring is still sitting there, and it's genuinely a nice piece of hardware.

You know something now that you didn't ten minutes ago. It measures a skill you can build for free, and your own tradition already wrote the manual. Everything the device promises to tell you, your body is already saying. You were just never taught the language, or you were taught to distrust it until a number agreed.

It comes down to one line. Before you buy the instrument, learn that you already are one.

One signal. Tomorrow morning. Before you touch your phone.

Pick one of the four and read it tomorrow before your phone gets a vote. Reply and tell me which one you chose and what it said. If enough of you ask, I'll go deep on a single reading next, ojas or agni, whichever the replies want.

title: Stop wishing your phone had a guest lock. It already has one.
text:
You can. You've been able to for years, and nobody ever showed you.

Last week I read a sharp little post titled "The phone features I can't believe we don't have." Top of the list: a guest lock that pins your phone to the app you're showing, and a way to hide photos from the camera roll. The writer wanted both. The comments nodded along. Of course we don't have that.

Except we do. Both of them. On iPhone and Android, shipped and sitting in Settings right now.

I know because I went to build the thing. I spent a day making a little app for exactly this handoff moment, and somewhere in the middle I realized I was rebuilding a feature Apple shipped in 2012. The app taught me something anyway, and I'll get to it. But the first lesson was blunt. The feature isn't missing. The knowledge is.

Three things below. The settings that already do "guest lock" and "hidden photos" on the phone in your hand. Why they stayed invisible this whole time. And the one case they genuinely don't cover, plus the fast fix for it. If you've ever done the hover-thumb handoff, this is for you.

When you can't do something on your phone, the story you tell yourself is that the feature doesn't exist. Apple hasn't built it. Android's too messy. Someday, maybe.

That story is wrong here, and it's wrong in a specific way. Guided Access, the iPhone feature that locks your phone to one app, shipped in 2012. Android's version, Screen Pinning, landed in 2014. They've been in every phone you've owned for more than a decade.

So why does everyone, including a writer sharp enough to publish a features wishlist, believe they're missing? Because they're buried. Guided Access hides under Settings, then Accessibility, three layers deep, behind a name that sounds like it's meant for someone else. Screen Pinning sits under Security behind a phrase nobody thinks to search. And even once you find them, arming them takes enough taps that you'll never reach for it in the five seconds you're actually handing the phone over.

That's the real problem. Not capability. Discovery, and friction at the worst possible moment. Which changes what you should do about it. Stop waiting for the feature. Go turn on the setting. And for the five-second case, get something faster than the setting.

The guest lock is already there

Pinning your phone to a single app is one gesture on both platforms.

On iPhone it's Guided Access. Turn it on once in Settings, then Accessibility, then Guided Access, and set a passcode. After that, open the photo or ticket you want to show, triple-click the side button, and the phone freezes on that screen. No swiping out, no home screen, no app switcher, until you triple-click again and enter your code. This is the exact guest lock the wishlist asked for.

On Android it's Screen Pinning. Settings, then Security, and flip it on. Open your app, swipe up to the recents view, tap the app's icon, and hit Pin. To leave, you hold Back and Recents together and unlock. Same idea, same result.

Turn one of them on right now, before you read the next part. Thirty seconds, and you'll have it forever.

The catch: it's fiddly to arm in the moment. Hold that thought.

Hidden photos are already there

Your private shots can be walled off from the camera roll without installing anything.

On Android, Google Photos has a Locked Folder. Anything you move into it drops out of the main grid and sits behind your fingerprint or PIN. A screenshot of your ID, a photo of a document, whatever you don't want surfacing when someone scrolls. Move it there and it's gone from the roll.

On iPhone there's a Hidden album, and on recent versions it's locked behind Face ID by default, along with Recently Deleted. Open Photos, scroll to Utilities, and you'll find the Hidden album that won't show its contents until your face clears it.

That's the second wish, granted. Do it now with three photos you'd rather nobody stumbled into.

The catch: this protects the whole library. Showing one photo still means handing over everything else.

Lock a single app behind your face

You can lock individual apps behind Face ID or a fingerprint, no third-party app, no sketchy download.

On iPhone with iOS 18, press and hold any app icon and you'll see Require Face ID. Turn it on and that app won't open for anyone but you, even when the phone is already unlocked. Messages, Photos, your banking app, your call.

Android has had versions of this for a while, and many phones from Samsung and others ship a built-in App Lock or Secure Folder in Settings. Same outcome. The app opens for you and nobody else.

People download shady "app locker" apps for exactly this, handing permissions to a stranger, when the phone does it natively. Lock one app now as a test.

The catch, and it's the one that ties all three together: every one of these takes a few taps to set up in the moment. Strong for the planned case. Too slow for the five-second one.

The one thing your phone doesn't do

Here's the gap none of the three fill cleanly. The everyday case. Someone's standing in front of you, you want to show them this one photo, right now, and you're not going to walk through Guided Access setup while they wait.

That's the thing I built. It's called Handoff. You pick the photo or photos you want to show, it opens them full screen in a locked viewer, and getting back out takes your PIN. Swipe all you like, you only ever see the ones you picked. It runs in the browser, installs to your home screen like a normal app, and every photo stays on your phone. Nothing uploads, no account, no server.

Now the honest part, because it's the whole point. A web app cannot block your phone's app switcher. Someone determined can still swipe up and out of it. I hit that wall building it, and it's exactly why the native features in the first three sections still matter. Handoff is for the friendly five-second handoff, the stranger checking your ticket. Guided Access is for the case where you actually don't trust the person holding your phone. Two layers, two jobs.

If I'd hidden that limit and sold it as a vault, you should have stopped trusting me. It isn't a vault. It's the fast lane for the low-stakes moment the native tools are too slow for. You can try it here.

Five minutes, once

Reading this changes nothing. Doing it takes five minutes, once.

Turn on Guided Access on iPhone, or Screen Pinning on Android. The menu paths are up in the first section. This is your real lock.

Move three photos you'd rather keep private into the Locked Folder on Android, or the Hidden album on iPhone.

Lock one app behind Face ID as a test, so the gesture is in your fingers when you need it.

Then hand your phone to someone in the room with one of these armed, and watch it hold. Feel how solid that is next to the hover-thumb you've been doing for years.

Last, for the quick case, try Handoff and feel the difference in speed. You'll land on your own rule fast. Native tools for anything that matters. Handoff for the five-second show.

The manual was missing, not the feature

Go back to that hovering thumb. All this time you thought your phone couldn't protect that moment, and the truth is it could. You were just never shown the screen. The feature wasn't missing. The manual was.

Your phone already does most of what you wish it did. The gap was never capability. It was that nobody walked you to the setting. So walk yourself there now. Open Settings and turn the lock on before you close this tab.

title: Stop asking AI to predict the market. Ask it to predict you.
text:
The number nobody selling that dream leads with: 87% of retail traders running automated systems lose money in their first year. That figure isn't from a hater. It's from a company that sells trading bots. When the people profiting off the fantasy quietly admit the fantasy loses, it's worth stopping.

And yet a handful of traders are making AI pay. They're doing something that looks backwards. They pointed it away from the market and at themselves.

I'm not going to tell you I cracked live crypto trading. I didn't. What I did was go looking, after the hundredth "autonomous trading agent" thread, for what works instead of what sounds good on launch day.

The trader who stopped me wasn't building an oracle at all. He had a vague suspicion about himself: after a big win, he'd get loose, take a trade or two he had no business taking. He'd felt it for years but never measured it. So he dumped his trade history into Claude and asked it to look.

He was, in his words, surprised how many times it happened and how much money he handed back making the same mistake over and over. Then he built a small bot that prompts him on every trade and reminds him of that pattern before he can repeat it.

That reframed the whole thing for me. The question was never "can AI predict the market?" The pros won that one, with faster data and machines you'll never match. The better question: what if I aimed it at the one thing I control?

Three things below. Why predicting the market is rigged against you. The reframe that needs no market edge. And a loop you can run this week with tools you already pay for. If you've watched a bot lose and suspected the real leak was closer to home, this is for you.

When you lose, you blame the strategy. Bad entry, wrong indicator, market's rigged. So you hunt for a better edge: sharper signals, a smarter model, more parameters.

What that story leaves out is where the money went. For most retail traders the loss isn't in the thesis at all, it's in the behavior wrapped around the thesis: the position you sized up because you were angry, the entry you chased because everyone was already in, the stop you slid because you couldn't stand being wrong.

You don't have to take my word for it. Journaling is the single habit almost every serious trader calls the most important thing they do, and almost nobody keeps it up. Ask why on any trading forum and the thread writes itself: everyone knows, nobody does it. And the damage underneath isn't subtle. There's an entire corner of Reddit, r/tradingpsychology, that exists because of it. "Lost everything to revenge trading" is a real post title. So is blowing up an account by sizing up after a loss.

The mistakes repeat. They're patterned. And a pattern in your own history is something you can find, if you point the right tool at it.

The leak is patterned

Start with the uncomfortable premise: your worst losses are probably a few behaviors you repeat, not a broken thesis.

Tilt, revenge trading, sizing up after a win, chasing tops. In the moment none of these feels like a pattern. Each one feels like this time being different, this setup being special. Stack ninety days of trades together and they stop looking special. They start looking like a schedule.

The trader I mentioned couldn't feel how often he over-risked after a win. He could only see it once something counted it for him. The leak is invisible at the level of a single trade and obvious across your full history.

So the first move isn't a better strategy. It's finding the leak.

Point the AI at yourself, not the market

The reframe: you cannot reliably beat the market, but you can reliably stop beating yourself. Only the second one is a game you can win.

Beating the market means out-trading firms with faster data and teams of quants. That's the game the 87% keep losing. Pointing AI at your own behavior is different. You're not competing with anyone. You're reading a dataset only you have, where the pattern is already sitting in plain sight, waiting for someone to count it.

Think mirror, not oracle. The oracle promises to tell you what the market will do, and it lies. The mirror tells you what you keep doing, and it's right, because the evidence is your own trades.

The reason this works now and didn't a few years ago is that the hard part collapsed. This used to mean obsessively diarizing every trade and being good at slicing your own data to find anything in it. Now it's two moves: log the trades, and ask Claude to compile them and tell you what you keep doing.

There's one catch. A mirror that only shows you the mistake after it happened is useful, but late.

The loop: log, find, nudge

The full loop is three steps, and it's the third one almost nobody ships.

One, log every trade automatically. If you trade perps, this is easy. The exchange APIs hand you the data. If you trade onchain, it's easier than you'd think, because the record is public and you can pull your wallet's history directly. The genuinely messy case is spreading across perps, spot, onchain, and a CEX at once, which is why most people give up and journal nothing.

Two, hand the log to Claude and ask what you keep doing. Not "how were my trades," but "what do I keep doing around wins, losses, and sizing, and what did each pattern cost me." Make it put a number on the leak. The number is what turns a vague feeling into something you can't unsee.

Three, the step that matters: turn each pattern into a rule that hits you before the next trade, not after. This is where the tools fall short. The sharpest thing I read in all of this was a trader saying a journal that only explains the mistake afterward is useful but late. Every polished AI trade journal does the after. Almost none do the before. And if you trade crypto, notice the gap: those journals are built for stock and futures traders. The onchain and perps crowd is barely served on the one step that counts.

Try it this week

You don't need to build anything yet. Try it on your own trades.

Pull your last thirty to ninety days. A perps API export, your onchain history, or a plain CSV, whatever you can get fastest. Hand it to Claude with one prompt: find my recurring behavioral patterns, especially around wins, losses, and position sizing, and estimate what each one cost me.

Then look for the single leak with the biggest number next to it. The trader's was over-risking after a win. Yours might be revenge entries, or holding losers too long, or piling in at tops. Check it against your gut. You probably already half-knew, which is why seeing it counted lands harder than any strategy tip.

Write that one pattern as a single if-then rule. "If I just closed a big win, no new position for thirty minutes." "If I'm adding to a loser, stop." Put it somewhere that reaches you at decision time, before the click. A sticky note, an alert, a bot that pings you, whatever you'll actually see. The goal isn't a dashboard. It's one behavior changed, with a number behind it.

The mirror, not the oracle

Forget the bot that prints money while you sleep. That's the oracle, and it has an 87% failure rate its own vendors admit to. The tool worth building is the mirror: the thing that catches you before you hand a good win back.

The edge you can get isn't over the market. It's over yourself. And the first step costs nothing but the export. Pull your log and ask what you keep doing.

Now I'm asking, because I want to know. Do you journal your trades? Really, or the way everyone means when they say they should? And would you use something that nudged you before you tilt, not after the money's gone? Or is that just me.

Reply and tell me. If enough of you say "shut up and take my money," that's the next thing I build.

title: The Most Dangerous Thing AI Can Automate Isn’t Coding
text:
He worries that working with LLMs is training him to spend more of his time skimming and judging rather than thinking slowly.

How to keep thinking

Imagine you're the guest on some kind of frenetic, software-engineering-themed game show. The host is constantly flipping over new cards with questions that you have to answer as fast as possible: Is this adjustment to the database schema right? Do these bits of data look plausible?

https://www.seangoedecke.com

I think he’s right.

But I think there’s a deeper problem underneath it.

The danger isn't simply that AI might make us think less.

It might make not thinking the rational choice.

The new shape of work

Goedecke describes working with AI as something like a frenetic software-engineering game show.

An agent gives you an architecture.

You judge it.

Another agent gives you an implementation.

You judge it.

Another gives you tests.

You judge those.

Then another proposes a completely different approach.

You compare.

Reject.

Accept.

Modify.

Delegate.

Repeat.

You can be extremely busy. You can even be highly skilled.

But the shape of your cognition has changed.

You're spending more time asking:

“Which of these answers is good?”

and less time asking:

“What do I actually think?”

That's not the same thing.

Goedecke calls this a shift toward the quick “skimming and judging” parts of the mind and away from the slower reflection required for deep thought and creativity. His solution is surprisingly old-fashioned: read difficult books and write in your own words.

I think that is only the beginning of the argument.

AI doesn't need to make you stupid

Imagine two people solving the same problem.

The first spends three hours trying to understand it.

They form a mental model (an internal map of how things work), make wrong guesses, discover contradictions, and eventually develop their own solution.

The second asks an AI for ten possible solutions.

They skim them.

They choose the best one.

Then they ask the AI to implement it.

The second person may be dramatically more productive.

And that's exactly the problem.

The second person may also be getting less practice at the thing that made the first person capable of solving novel problems in the first place.

This isn't an argument against AI.

It's an argument about training.

If you stop lifting weights because a machine can move the weight for you, you haven't disproved the value of strength. You've simply stopped training it.

The same may be true of cognition.

If AI increasingly performs the generation, exploration, explanation, implementation, and even criticism, what remains for the human?

Selection.

“Option three looks best.”

That's a useful skill.

But selection is not the same as understanding.

The economic problem is worse

Here's where I think Goedecke's argument deserves to be pushed further.

Suppose deep thinking makes you better at your job.

But suppose another person uses AI aggressively and produces ten times as much visible output.

Who does the company reward?

Usually, the second person.

Not because the company is evil.

Because the incentive is obvious.

If technology gives everyone a “make this ten times faster” button, refusing to press it can become a competitive disadvantage. Goedecke makes essentially this point himself: people are heavily incentivized to use these tools when their peers are doing so.

So this isn't merely a personal discipline problem.

It is a system problem (a problem created by the surrounding rules).

AI can create an environment where:

speed → more output → more reward → more speed

And then the environment selects for people who are increasingly good at managing AI output.

The loop reinforces itself.

Eventually, deep thinking becomes something you have to protect outside the workday.

That's exactly what Goedecke predicts when he says we may need to find ways outside work to maintain the habit of thinking slowly.

And that possibility is much stranger than “AI makes us lazy.”

The real scarce resource isn't answers

For most of human history, information was scarce.

Then the internet made information abundant.

Now AI is making answers abundant.

So what becomes scarce?

Judgment.

But even that isn't quite enough.

Because judgment requires something underneath it.

You need to know:

What problem are we actually solving?

Is this even the right problem?

What assumptions are hidden here?

What do I believe?

What tradeoff am I willing to make?

What outcome actually matters?

What should I refuse to optimize?

AI can help with all of these questions.

But there is a crucial difference between using AI to interrogate your thinking and using AI instead of thinking.

The first expands your mind.

The second can gradually turn your mind into a review interface.

Don't outsource the formation of your worldview

This is where I think the conversation about AI needs a better rule.

We keep asking:

“What should humans still do?”

That's the wrong question.

A better question is:

“What should remain ours?”

Let AI handle things that are mechanical, repetitive, searchable, testable, or easily reversible.

Let it explore possibilities.

Let it generate drafts.

Let it write code.

Let it summarize ten papers.

Let it attack your argument.

Let it give you perspectives you hadn't considered.

But be careful about outsourcing the parts that determine the direction of your life.

What problem is worth solving.

What you actually believe.

What you value.

What risks you're willing to take.

What kind of person you're trying to become.

What kind of world you're trying to help create.

Those aren't merely tasks.

They're acts of authorship (choosing what your life means and does).

And if you outsource enough of them, you may become extraordinarily effective at living a life you never consciously chose.

There's a useful distinction here

Think about two workflows.

The first:

Ask → receive → accept → execute.

This makes AI your substitute.

The second:

Think → write → ask → challenge → revise → decide.

This makes AI your adversary and collaborator (something that helps you test yourself).

The difference is enormous.

Before asking AI, try to form your own answer.

Write it down.

Then ask AI to attack it.

Find where you're wrong.

Ask what you're missing.

Generate alternatives.

Then make the final judgment yourself.

This creates a productive tension (useful pressure between opposing ideas).

You're not protecting your brain from AI.

You're using AI to make your brain work harder.

Why writing matters so much

This is also why Goedecke's recommendation to write in your own words is more profound than it initially sounds.

When you say:

“I have an idea.”

you often don't.

You have a feeling that an idea exists somewhere nearby.

Writing forces you to find it.

A vague intuition becomes a sentence.

The sentence creates a contradiction.

The contradiction forces another distinction.

The distinction reveals an assumption.

The assumption turns out to be wrong.

And suddenly you understand something you didn't understand when you started.

The writing wasn't communication after the thinking.

The writing was the thinking.

That's why having AI write the whole thing for you can be subtly dangerous, even when the final article is better.

You may end up with a polished expression of an idea you never fully constructed.

The artifact improves.

The thinker doesn't necessarily improve with it.

Goedecke makes essentially this point when he says that putting words together yourself forces you to articulate your thoughts, and that the idea itself is often constructed during writing.

The question isn't “AI or no AI?”

That debate is already obsolete.

The better question is:

Which cognitive muscles should I automate, and which should I deliberately keep exercising?

I don't want to manually perform every task AI can perform.

That would be ridiculous.

I want AI to remove the boring parts so I can spend more time on the interesting parts.

But there's a catch.

You don't always know which parts are boring until you've become good at them.

Learning architecture may feel slow.

Writing may feel inefficient.

Reading a difficult book may feel painfully unproductive compared with asking an AI for its summary.

Sitting alone with a problem for two hours can feel absurd when an AI can give you twelve plausible answers in thirty seconds.

But that friction may be doing something.

It may be building the very capacity that allows you to recognize which of those twelve answers is actually worth taking seriously.

The deeper question: which problems remain yours?

This is the part I find most interesting.

If AI can increasingly solve problems, the defining human advantage may shift from solving problems to choosing problems.

And choosing problems is not a trivial optimization problem.

Your life is partly the collection of problems you decide are worth suffering for.

Some problems make you smaller.

Others force you to grow.

Some are assigned to you by institutions, employers, algorithms, parents, or culture.

Others are chosen.

The difference matters.

Because once AI can solve almost anything, the question becomes:

What deserves to be solved?

And then:

Why should I care?

And finally:

What kind of life am I building by spending my limited attention on this problem?

Those questions cannot be delegated without consequences.

You can ask AI for its answer.

You shouldn't let it quietly become the author of yours.

The new rule

So I don't think the lesson from Goedecke's essay is:

“Stop using AI.”

It's almost the opposite.

Use it aggressively.

But maintain a part of your life where you are forced to think without it.

Read things that are difficult.

Write things that nobody asked you to write.

Sit with problems before asking for solutions.

Form your own hypothesis before seeing the model's answer.

Argue with the machine.

Let it argue back.

And occasionally experience the uncomfortable sensation of having absolutely no idea what you think.

That's usually where thinking begins.

Because the real danger isn't that AI will think for us.

It's that AI will become so good at thinking on demand that we stop noticing when we've stopped thinking for ourselves.

The future may not belong to people who refuse to use AI.

It may belong to people who know when not to.

And perhaps even more importantly:

people who still know what is worth thinking about.

title: Your Community's Moderation Bot Shouldn't Have a Single Point of Failure
text:
A channel grows past the point humans can read everything. Someone bolts on an AI agent to classify spam. It works. Six months later, the community's moderation depends on one company's pricing, one company's terms of service, one company's idea of acceptable content.

Nobody planned that. It's just the default path in 2026: call a centralized AI API.

Wrote up why that's a contradiction worth fixing, and an architecture that fixes it.

Providers change their usage policies regularly. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google have all done it more than once in the past two years. Moderation is the awkward workload too: to classify spam you have to send spam through the API, and developers running abuse-processing bots have hit opaque account suspensions even after doing everything right.

The community chose a permissionless protocol specifically to avoid platform risk. Then reintroduced it one layer up, in the tooling. No headline censorship. The bot just quietly stops working.

One caveat before the fix, because protocol-literate people will raise it anyway: Farcaster channels are a client-level construct, not protocol-level. Moderation state lives in the client, not the network. So no, decentralizing the AI layer doesn't purify the whole stack.

That's not a hole in the argument, it's the argument. The channel-layer gap is native and openly debated. The AI dependency is different: it's being added right now, bot by bot, outside anyone's control, and nobody's watching it.

The fix, five parts, only one of them new:

1. Client integration watches the channel (unchanged)

2. Agent orchestrator owns the logic, does zero inference itself

3. Compute router sends jobs to decentralized GPU networks like Nosana, picking a market by price/queue/latency

4. Independent GPU operators run open-weights models, return a classification

5. Orchestrator acts: hide, flag, allow, or queue for human review Degraded mode always falls to human review, never silent auto-removal. The community's authority is the floor, not a feature bolted on top.

The part every decentralized AI pitch wants to skip: why trust a random GPU node's answer? Spot-checking helps against faults, not against someone running multiple correlated nodes. Majority voting costs N times more and assumes independence, the first thing a cheap attack breaks. Reputation and staking/slashing help more, but they're hard, especially for something as subjective as moderation.

Honest answer: good enough for spam today (low stakes, recoverable, human review catches the rest). Not solved for high-stakes calls. Narrower claim than "decentralized AI is trustless," and one I can defend.

Steelman the other side: centralized APIs are cheaper, faster, better documented, better at nuance. All true, and beside the point. This class of tool is bought for its guarantees, not its throughput. A community that picked a censorship-resistant protocol is making a statement about who can shut things down. Reintroducing a shutdown switch one layer up doesn't serve that just because it's cheaper this quarter.

The protocol layer is being decentralized in the open, gap by gap. The tooling layer is where the quiet re-centralization is happening, one API key at a time.

title: Samjha Do
text:
समझा दो

Samjha Do means "make me understand." Last week I built an app with that name. It does one thing. You describe a screen that is confusing you, and it explains what is happening in calm Hindi or Marathi, as text and as a voice you can listen to.

I built it for a hackathon run by Mesh API. I also built it for someone in my family who cannot see, and for every parent who has ever called their child in a panic because a message on their phone said something frightening.

If you grew up translating technology for your family, you know the call. "There is a message asking for an OTP. Should I give it?" The answer matters. Sometimes the message is the bank doing its job. Sometimes it is a thief. The whole reason this app exists is that it can tell those two apart. Describe a real one time password request and it explains, calmly, what to do. Describe the scam version and it tells you, gently and clearly, to stop.

What it is, honestly

The app is small. It is one Cloudflare Worker and a single web page. The thinking is done by Mesh API. One model writes the explanation. A second model, a voice model called Bulbul from Sarvam, reads that explanation aloud in Hindi or Marathi. Both sit behind one key.

It took four days. The deadline was seven. By the time I submitted it, the total cost of all the AI work across forty eight test requests was eleven cents.

I am telling you the cost because the loud advice online right now is to build an AI agent and get rich. The part those threads skip is where the real work happens. It is not in the model. It is in everything around it.

Where the work actually was

My laptop is a 2015 MacBook Air with four gigabytes of memory. It cannot run the local test server that a normal build would use. So every time I needed to check my work, I deployed the app to the live internet and tested it there. That kept me honest, because I was always looking at the real thing and not a copy of it.

I attacked my own app before the judges could. I asked it questions it was never meant to answer. Most of the time it refused correctly. But when I asked it something with no screen at all, like a plain trivia question, it invented a fake screen and explained that instead. That is the exact failure that would embarrass the app in front of a real user. I found it, fixed it that evening, deployed the fix, and tested until the invention was gone and nothing else had broken.

I measured the speed instead of hoping. An explanation takes about six seconds. The voice takes about eight seconds to start. I did not pretend those seconds do not exist. I built the demo so that it talks through the wait, which also proves, live, that the app is really calling the service and not faking it.

The moment I made the code public, I realized the way the app talks to Mesh was now public too. Anyone could call it. So I put a hard spending limit on the account. No amount of stranger traffic can run up a bill I did not agree to.

None of that is exciting. All of it is the difference between a demo and something a member of your family can actually use without you standing next to them.

Why this is the niche

The results of the hackathon are not out yet. Mesh API already gave the project a public mention, which meant more to me than I expected. But the app does not need a prize to be useful. It is live right now at samjha-do.kazani.workers.dev. The code is open. The next confusing screen your mother sees has an answer that does not require her to phone you first.

Small agents that do one specific thing, built for the people the industry usually forgets, are where I want to spend my time. Not a general assistant. Not a platform. One clear job, done in a language and a voice the person actually trusts, with the scam caught before it costs them anything.

That is the whole idea. I intend to stay with it.

title: The 17.9% Problem: Why LLM Agents Need Real Feedback, Not Self-Verification
text:
The experiment

The researchers built ComPilot — a system that uses an LLM to optimize loops in C programs. The LLM proposes transformation sequences (tile this loop, parallelize that one, interchange these two), a compiler applies them, and the program runs on real hardware. The speedup gets fed back to the LLM, which uses it to decide what to try next.

The result: 3.54x geometric mean speedup over unoptimized code across 150 benchmarks, beating the state-of-the-art polyhedral optimizer (Pluto) on 79% of test cases. Off-the-shelf Gemini Flash. No fine-tuning.

That's impressive but not the interesting part.

The interesting part

To validate the design, they ran an ablation: instead of emitting compiler API commands and getting formal legality checks, have the LLM just rewrite the code directly. Verify correctness by comparing output to the original.

This is what most LLM coding tools implicitly do. Write the code, run the tests, check if it passes.

Result: 14–16% lower speedup, 5.3x more tokens consumed — and 17.9% of "correct" transformations were semantically wrong under random inputs, despite passing the original test.

The code looked right. The tests passed. The program was broken.

This isn't a compiler-specific failure mode. It's a grounding failure mode. If the only feedback signal available to an agent is "does the output look plausible," you will get confident, silent wrongness at a non-trivial rate.

What actually fixed it

Formal legality checking via the compiler's dependence analysis. Not output comparison. Not asking the LLM to double-check. Delegating verification to something that can actually verify.

And then: measuring real execution time and feeding that number back.

Two separate signals, both essential:

Is this transformation legal? — answered by the compiler, not the LLM

Is it faster? — answered by the hardware, not a cost model

The LLM's job is exploration and strategy. The environment's job is ground truth. Mix those up and you get the 17.9% problem.

The feedback loop ablation

They also tested removing feedback entirely — let the LLM propose transformations but don't tell it what happened. Blind search.

Single-run speedup dropped 23%. With GPT-4o it dropped 40%.

This is the part worth sitting with. The performance difference between "LLM with feedback" and "LLM without feedback" is larger than the difference between any two LLMs in their comparison. GPT-4o with feedback beats GPT-o3-mini without it.

The model choice matters less than whether the model can observe the consequences of its actions.

What this means for agent design

Three things I take from this:

1. Self-verification is load-bearing in ways that break silently. If your agent validates its own output — by re-reading it, running it against a single test, checking if it looks right — you have a 17.9% silent failure rate floor, minimum. The exact number will vary by domain, but the failure mode is structural.

2. Delegate verification to the environment, not the model. Wherever there's a formal check available — type system, schema validation, compiler, database constraint, test suite with random inputs — use it. Don't ask the LLM to reason about correctness. Route the action through something that actually enforces it.

3. The feedback signal quality is the ceiling on agent performance. ComPilot's feedback is unusually clean: binary legality + continuous speedup ratio, measured on real hardware. Most agents have murkier feedback — user ratings, task completion proxies, soft metrics. The messier the feedback, the harder it is for the agent to learn from it in-context. Designing clear feedback signals is underrated agent infrastructure work.

The meta-point

The paper's framing is compiler optimization. The actual contribution is an empirical demonstration that feedback-grounded agentic loops work, and a controlled ablation showing exactly how much each component contributes.

Most agent papers either show a capability ("the LLM can do X") or benchmark a prompt strategy. This one answers "what does the loop buy you" and "what breaks if you remove formal verification" with actual numbers.

That's rare. The numbers are:

Feedback vs. no feedback: +23–40% performance

Formal verification vs. output comparison: –18% correctness failures eliminated, –14% performance gap closed

If you're building anything where agents take actions with real consequences, those numbers are the architecture argument you've been looking for.

title: Bodies together, Minds elsewhere.
text:
How screens have changed in-person connection?

Screens let us edit, delay, and curate interaction. That trains the nervous system to expect control.

Face-to-face interaction is the opposite: real-time, uneditable, full of micro-risk (tone, pauses, eye contact).

So when people say “in-person feels harder now,” it’s often because:

They’ve practiced low-risk communication

And deconditioned themselves from live emotional feedback

This isn’t weakness - it’s conditioning. We haven’t lost the capacity for deep in-person connection. We’ve lost conditioning

Attention fragmentation leaks into presence

Screens train:

Rapid context switching

Partial attention

Constant novelty scanning

In person, presence requires:

Sustained attention

Tolerating silence

Tracking subtle cues

So even when two people are physically together, their attention habits may still be optimized for screens, not humans.

This creates a mismatch:

Bodies together, minds elsewhere.

Just like physical strength:

Use it → it feels natural

Don’t use it → it feels awkward, effortful, even anxiety-provoking

Awkwardness is not a flaw. It’s a signal of underused capacity.

We notice:

Awkward dinners

People on phones

Shallow small talk

We miss:

The fact that when phones are put away intentionally, connection often deepens faster than before

That many people now crave depth more intensely because screens made superficiality obvious

So the story isn’t:

“Screens ruined connection.”

It’s closer to:

“Screens raised the contrast between shallow and real connection.”

Screens didn’t destroy our ability to connect.

They exposed how much connection depends on trained attention and emotional tolerance.

In other words:

Screens changed the default

Not the ceiling

The people who rebuild:

Attention stamina

Comfort with silence

Embodied presence

often report deeper in-person connection than pre-screen life, because it’s now chosen, not accidental.

Face-to-face connection has always required capacity:

Emotional regulation

Listening without escape

Being seen without filters

Screens didn’t remove those requirements.

They just gave us a way to avoid training for them.

Avoidance feels easier, until you try to return.

title: Privacy doesn't mean anything anymore, anonymity does
text:
1. "Privacy" has been hollowed out

In modern tech, privacy is mostly a policy promise, not a technical constraint.

If a system:

- collects identifiers

- stores metadata

- logs access

- can be compelled to disclose

Then "privacy" is conditional trust, not protection.

Most "privacy-first" products are doing risk management, not risk elimination.

That's not cynicism; that's architecture.

2. Anonymity is architectural, not moral

True anonymity means:

- the system cannot know

- therefore it cannot leak

- therefore it cannot comply

This is the only model that survives coercion.

If a service could identify you under pressure, it eventually will. Law, breach, insider threat, or acquisition - pick one.

3. The "Privacy Theater Playbook" describes how services collect user data incrementally through email registration, password resets, phone verification, and identity confirmation, despite privacy policy claims.

Incremental identity accretion is exactly how most systems launder surveillance while maintaining plausible deniability:

"Just an email"

"Just for recovery"

"Just for abuse prevention"

"Just for compliance"

Each step seems reasonable in isolation.

In aggregate, it recreates full-spectrum identity.

That's not accidental. It's incentive-aligned.

4. Possession = vulnerability

This is the core law most people refuse to internalize:

"If you hold the data, you are the risk surface."

No amount of encryption, policy language, or goodwill overrides that.

The safest data is data that never existed.

Privacy still matters - just not as a primary defense.

Privacy today means:

- data minimization

- compartmentalization

- harm reduction

It's a damage control layer, not a shield.

The term "privacy" in tech is often misused as a marketing tactic rather than an architectural reality, with many services collecting extensive user data while claiming to protect privacy.

True anonymity is an architectural decision that makes it technically impossible to compromise or identify users, even under duress or legal orders.

The core vulnerability in most services is possession of user data; services that do not collect or store certain data cannot leak or be forced to reveal it.

Mullvad VPN exemplifies real anonymity by using randomly generated account numbers instead of personal information, rendering them unable to comply with data requests.

Email addresses are identified as a primary mechanism that destroys anonymity due to their role as identity markers, trackability, persistence, and susceptibility to social engineering.

Crypto payments are accepted to decouple transactions from persistent identity, as traditional payment systems create surveillance infrastructure, though traditional payment options are also pragmatically supported.

5. Crypto ≠ anonymity by default

- Public blockchains are anti-anonymity by design

- Pseudonymity collapses under correlation

- Crypto payments only help if the entire stack respects anonymity

Otherwise crypto becomes the most permanent surveillance ledger ever created.

Anonymity is distinguished from impunity, security, invisibility, and zero trust, emphasizing that it's about architectural limitations on data collection to minimize damage when trust fails, not a license for illegal activity or complete invulnerability.

Privacy without anonymity is a promise.

Anonymity is a constraint.

Most users fail not because they misunderstand anonymity, but because they achieve it in one layer and leak it in another.

Email is one such leak - but not the only one:

- timing correlations

- writing style

- device fingerprinting

- payment rails

- social graph leakage

Anonymity is about not creating irreversible power asymmetry.

It's a defensive posture against:

- future regime change

- policy drift

- data reuse

- retroactive enforcement

- adversaries you haven't met yet

That temporal dimension is often missed.

6. Most products will never choose anonymity by default because:

- it breaks growth analytics

- it breaks personalization

- it breaks monetization

- it breaks compliance narratives

- it breaks VC expectations

Which means:

"Anonymity will not be mass-adopted. It will be selectively adopted by people who understand power."

That"s the real dividing line.
